Where are Chicagoans allowed to live?

For a century, Chicago has had a set of laws, called zoning, that regulate what kinds of housing can be built where. And for nearly a century, reforms to those laws moved in one direction: Fewer homes and smaller buildings. City leaders wanted to be more like the suburbs, where many residents—especially white, middle class, and high-income residents—were fleeing.

An engine for exclusion

Especially after 1970, Chicago’s City Council repeatedly prohibited three-flats and other apartment buildings where they had previously been allowed. In other places where apartments were allowed, they required them to be smaller. These changes, called “downzones,” disproportionately happened in higher-income and majority-white communities. Research has found that where these downzones took place, housing costs rose and the population of people of color fell.

Forty-one percent

Today, 41% of Chicago—and almost two-thirds of residential land—prohibits apartments or condos of any kind. As a result, the easiest type of housing to build in most of the city is the most expensive kind: single-family homes.

One alderperson, one veto, one building at a time

As a result, apartments or condos—including affordable housing—almost always need a zoning change to be built. Under a system called “aldermanic prerogative,” the local alderperson can approve or veto these developments. Traditionally, alderpeople would only consider changing zoning in response to individual development proposals, making broader community planning extremely difficult, increasing costs, slowing down development of affordable and multifamily housing, and opening the door to real or perceived corruption.

From reactive to proactive

Starting in 2024, a growing number of alderpeople began working with the Department of Planning and Development to make community plans, and then rezone a corridor or part of a neighborhood to match those plans. This is a major change in how Chicago regulates new housing, even though other cities have been doing it for decades.

Western Avenue: North Center and Lincoln Square

The very first of these rezonings took place in fall 2024. Following a public engagement process to complete the Western Avenue Corridor Study, more than 600 properties across five miles were rezoned to allow more apartments and affordable housing.

Cottage Grove: Bronzeville

One of the first major South Side rezonings designated half a mile in Bronzeville as B3-3, allowing mixed-use buildings of roughly five stories. This designation became common for rezoned neighborhood commercial streets.

Missing Middle: Chatham, South Chicago, and Morgan Park

In addition to neighborhood commercial streets, some rezonings have been applied to residential side streets. Together, several “missing middle” ordinances rezoned 805 vacant city-owned lots to RT-4 to allow two- and three-flats.

35th Street: McKinley Park

While allowing more multifamily and affordable housing has been a goal of most rezonings, some are aimed almost exclusively at neighborhood business development. In McKinley Park, alderpeople rezoned a historic community business street to allow new shops after previous representatives had used zoning to ensure any new business—not just new building—would need their approval to open.

Broadway: Uptown and Edgewater

Most of the rezonings have been enacted with little organized opposition. Broadway is an exception, particularly in the Edgewater section, which is one of the only places where a rezoning has taken place in a majority-white area. The Broadway rezoning also allowed a higher density than other rezonings, with many parcels designated B3-5, which allows mixed-use buildings of about seven stories.

In perspective

While the new community planning efforts that include rezoning are a significant development in Chicago’s land use, they have also left the vast majority of the city untouched, even in neighborhoods where they have taken place. Most are limited to commercial streets that were already relatively dense and served by transit. All side-street rezonings—those that allow two- and three-flats in neighborhoods that previously banned them—have taken place on the South Side.

Learning from other cities

Other cities, like Seattle and New York, have been doing proactive rezonings for years. Those cities have had success by coordinating rezonings across communities; rezoning more higher-income communities as well as lower-income ones; and standardizing more inclusive and streamlined public input processes.

The Chicago region

While this memo focuses on the City of Chicago, a mirror approach is necessary at the regional and state level to allow more kinds of housing, especially in affluent communities. The Affordable Housing Planning and Appeal Act (AHPAA) was designed to be one way to do this, but needs to be strengthened. The BUILD package is another such proposal.
